extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of UK employment law (lawyers, judges, law students)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal guidance from Nelson v BBC (No 2) on when an employee's conduct amounts to contributory fault in an unfair dismissal claim and the test for reducing damages; also discusses the 'contract test' approach to redundancy used by the Court of Appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of Appeal three-stage test for contributory fault
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court of Appeal laid out a three-stage test to whether there is contributory fault in an unfair dismissal claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is: (1) Was the employee culpable or blameworthy? (2) Did the employee's actions cause or contribute to the dismissal? (3) Is it just and equitable in the circumstances to reduce the award? Example application: Brandon LJ held that Mr Nelson's behaviour, described as "perverse or foolish … or … bloody minded", reduced his damages to zero despite the dismissal being technically unfair. Use the three questions in sequence — culpability, causation/contribution, and the discretionary 'just and equitable' assessment — when deciding whether, and by how much, to reduce an unfair dismissal award for contributory fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract test for redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an employee was 'redundant' is to be determined by reference to the terms (explicit or implied) in their employment contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by the Court of Appeal in Nelson v BBC (No 2) as a method of assessing redundancy (i.e., examine contractual terms to see whether work has diminished or ceased). Note: this 'contract test', together with the related 'function test', was subsequently rejected by the House of Lords in Murray v Foyle Meats Ltd, so be aware of later authoritative developments when relying on this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of employee misconduct on damages in unfair dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee misconduct or unreasonable behaviour can reduce or extinguish compensation even where dismissal is technically unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Nelson v BBC (No 2) the employee's 'bloody minded' refusal to accept a transfer led the court to reduce his damages to zero. This illustrates that contributory fault can operate to reduce awards and that the factual nature and degree of an employee's blameworthiness are central to the 'just and equitable' assessment under the three-stage test.
